blurb: Wall of Sound to Thriller: the pop songs everyone knows, and how they were made.

stories.title: Good Vibrations
stories.dek: A pocket symphony built from pieces
stories.body:
By 1966 Brian Wilson was no longer touring with the Beach Boys. The band was on the road playing surf and car songs while he stayed home in California writing and producing. After the album Pet Sounds, he wanted to make something even more ambitious: a single that would be a small symphony.

He later said the idea came from his mother, who once told him that dogs bark at some people because they can sense their vibrations. The thought stuck. Wilson began to write a song about feelings that could be felt but not seen, and he decided to make the recording in pieces. Over several months he worked at studios across Los Angeles, including Gold Star, Western and Columbia. At each one he recorded a different section of music with the Los Angeles studio players sometimes called the Wrecking Crew. Each studio had its own sound, and Wilson used that to his advantage.

The recording included cellos, organ and an unusual instrument called the electro-theremin. It was not a true theremin, but it produced a similar sweeping, eerie whistle. The musician who played it, Paul Tanner, was a former trombonist from the Glenn Miller orchestra who had helped design the device. That sound became the song's hook and gave listeners a strange, thrilling shiver.

Wilson then edited the sections together on tape into a three-and-a-half-minute record. Mike Love wrote the final lyrics. The cost of the recording was reportedly enormous for a single in that era. When Capitol Records released it in October 1966, the song soared to the top of the charts in both the United States and Britain.

For Wilson, it should have been a triumph. He began work on a larger album, called Smile, which was meant to build on the same ideas. But the project proved difficult. The band argued, Wilson grew anxious, and the recording was shelved in 1967. For decades the music circulated only among fans. Wilson finally completed a new version in 2004, and the original sessions were released in 2011 as The Smile Sessions.

"Good Vibrations" remained the single piece that showed what he had been aiming for. It proved that a pop record could be built like a film score, from many small parts, and that a three-minute song could be as daring as anything in rock.

stories.title: ABBA
stories.dek: From Eurovision to a worldwide sound
stories.body:
In the early 1970s two Swedish songwriters, Björn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson, were looking for a way to become known outside their country. Each had been in a popular band at home. They met in 1966 and began writing together. Björn married a singer, Agnetha Fältskog, in 1971, and Benny was with another singer, Anni-Frid Lyngstad, known as Frida. The four were two couples, and they began recording together.

Their manager, Stig Anderson, saw a way forward in the Eurovision Song Contest, a televised event watched across Europe. In 1973 they entered a song and finished third in the Swedish selection. A year later they tried again with "Waterloo", a rousing song with a thumping beat. On April 6, 1974, in Brighton, England, the group appeared in glittery costumes and won. Eurovision had rarely launched a career this large, and the song became a hit across Europe.

ABBA, a name made from the initials of their first names, then went on a remarkable run. They recorded in Stockholm, and later at their own Polar Studios. They wrote their own songs, with Björn on lyrics and Benny on music, and they spent weeks perfecting a sound of layered voices, bright keyboards and a clear, polished mix.

In June 1976 they performed a new song, "Dancing Queen," on a television gala in Stockholm on the eve of the wedding of King Carl XVI Gustaf and Silvia Sommerlath. It was a soaring song with a classic piano opening. It became one of the group's best-known recordings, and it remains a staple of dance floors and weddings.

The group's songs grew more emotional as the years passed. Both marriages ended, and their lives were in the public eye. Yet they continued to release strong work, including the album Super Trouper in 1980, until the group stopped working together in the early 1980s.

Interest in the music never faded. In 1999 a stage musical, Mamma Mia!, put their songs into a new story. It ran for years in London and around the world and later became a hit film. A group that began as an entry in a song contest had become part of the world's shared pop memory.

stories.title: Elton John and Bernie Taupin
stories.dek: Two strangers, one envelope of lyrics
stories.body:
In 1967 two young men answered the same advertisement in a British music paper. Liberty Records was looking for new songwriters. One was Reginald Dwight, a piano player from the London suburbs who had been playing in a band and had a gift for melody. The other was Bernie Taupin, a teenager from Lincolnshire who wrote verses about the American West but had no music. The label's talent scout saw that they were a perfect match, though neither had met the other.

They began to work together by mail. Taupin would write lyrics and send them to Dwight, who by then was calling himself Elton John, and Elton would set them to music. That was how they worked for decades. They seldom wrote in the same room. According to a story that John has often told, he wrote the tune for "Your Song" in about twenty minutes.

Success came in 1970. In August Elton John played his first American show at the Troubadour in Los Angeles. Before an audience that included music-industry people he pounded the piano, leapt around the stage and sang with an energy that few had expected. The next morning, reviews called him a star. His album Elton John and its single "Your Song" were hits.

A string of albums followed. Honky Château in 1972 included "Rocket Man," a song that Taupin has said was inspired by a Ray Bradbury story. Goodbye Yellow Brick Road in 1973 included "Candle in the Wind," Taupin's tribute to Marilyn Monroe. In the mid-1970s John was among the biggest stars in the world, known for oversized glasses and feathered costumes.

The partnership continued to produce hits. In 1997, after the death of Princess Diana, Taupin rewrote the words of "Candle in the Wind" for her funeral, and Elton sang it at Westminster Abbey. The record was among the best-selling singles of all time.

The two men remained friends and collaborators for more than fifty years. The pairing remains one of the most successful songwriting partnerships in popular music.

stories.title: Close to You
stories.dek: How the Carpenters found their sound with a song nobody wanted
stories.body:
Karen and Richard Carpenter grew up in New Haven, Connecticut, and moved with their parents to Downey, California, in 1963. Richard played piano and arranged; Karen, a few years younger, played drums and, as it turned out, had one of the most distinctive voices in pop. After years of local gigs and a demo tape, they were signed in 1969 by A&M Records, the label that trumpet player Herb Alpert had started with Jerry Moss.

Their first album did not set the world on fire. Then, in 1970, Alpert suggested a song he thought might suit them. It was "(They Long to Be) Close to You", written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David, and it was already known. Singer Richard Chamberlain had recorded it in 1963, and Dionne Warwick, among others, had sung it too. None of those versions had found a large audience.

Richard changed the arrangement. He built a gentle, steady rhythm and set Karen's low, warm voice at the front, with the group's multi-tracked harmonies behind her. In the studio, Richard has said, he and Karen layered their voices many times to produce a sound like a small choir. The record has no flash at all, and that was the point. When it was released that summer, it caught on quickly on the radio, helped by a wistful quality that made listeners feel it was meant for them alone.

The song launched a remarkable run. "We've Only Just Begun" followed, born of a bank commercial, then "Superstar" and "Rainy Days and Mondays". Between 1970 and the end of the decade the duo recorded a long string of soft-pop favorites, and they were a regular presence on American radio. Critics were sometimes cool, but their records were beautifully made, and the voice at the heart of them had an unusual honesty.

Karen died in February 1983, at only 32, of heart failure linked to anorexia nervosa. Her death helped bring the illness wider attention. Richard kept her recordings in circulation, and the songs from those years still sound as warm as they did when they first reached the radio.

stories.title: Making Thriller
stories.dek: Quincy Jones, a guitar favor and the album that broke records
stories.body:
When Michael Jackson was 21, he already had a childhood as a star behind him. He wanted to make a record that no one would mistake for the work of a former child singer. In 1979 he turned to Quincy Jones, a veteran arranger who had worked with Frank Sinatra and Count Basie, and the result, Off the Wall, was a bright, sophisticated album. It included "Rock with You", written by Rod Temperton, an English keyboardist who had come to Jones's attention through the band Heatwave.

Jackson and Jones made a second album with higher ambitions. Thriller came out in November 1982. Temperton wrote the title track, and the horror-movie star Vincent Price spoke the rap that closes it. Jackson wrote "Billie Jean" and "Beat It" himself. Jones has said he asked Jackson to shorten the long opening of "Billie Jean", and Jackson insisted that the groove was the point. Jones gave in.

"Beat It" was meant to bring rock listeners into the record. Jones reached out to Eddie Van Halen, the guitarist of Van Halen, who came to the studio and, by his own account, played the solo as a favor, with no pay. He has said that he first thought the call might be a prank. Toto's Steve Lukather and Jeff Porcaro played on the track as well, and the song fused rock guitar with a dance rhythm in a way few records had managed.

The video for "Thriller", directed by John Landis, followed in December 1983. It ran close to 14 minutes and was staged like a horror film. Music television had been a small channel only a couple of years before, and Jackson's clips helped turn it into an event for a broad audience.

At the 1984 Grammy Awards, Thriller won eight awards, a record at the time. The album stayed on the charts for years. For Jones and Jackson, who had both been told that they had done enough, it showed that a pop album could be made with the care of a film score and the energy of a street dance.

stories.title: The Stranger
stories.dek: Billy Joel, Phil Ramone and a ballad that almost got cut
stories.body:
By 1977 Billy Joel had already learned how hard the record business could be. His first album, Cold Spring Harbor, was released with the tape running too fast, so that his voice sounded higher than it had. He fled to Los Angeles, played piano in a bar under the name Bill Martin, and then signed with Columbia. Piano Man, in 1973, gave him a hit, but his next albums sold only modestly.

For his fifth album, Joel wanted a change. He had a touring band that knew his songs, and he wanted a producer who could capture them in the studio. He found Phil Ramone, a New York engineer and producer who had worked with Paul Simon and Burt Bacharach. Ramone recorded Joel with his own players, including drummer Liberty DeVitto and saxophonist Richie Cannata, rather than with hired hands, and he gave the sound a polish that Joel's earlier records had lacked.

The album, The Stranger, held a series of New York stories. "Movin' Out (Anthony's Song)" was about the working-class ambitions of his neighbors. "Only the Good Die Young" teased a Catholic girl, and drew complaints from some Catholic groups and a few radio stations. Joel has said the controversy only helped the song. "Scenes from an Italian Restaurant" ran like a small movie in three parts.

One song nearly stayed off the album. "Just the Way You Are" was a quiet ballad that Joel had written for his wife and manager, Elizabeth Weber. He reportedly thought it was too soft, but Linda Ronstadt and Phoebe Snow, who heard it in the studio, urged him to keep it. Ramone asked the jazz saxophonist Phil Woods to play an alto solo, and Woods's airy melody became one of the most recognizable lines on the record.

"Just the Way You Are" won the Grammy Awards for Record of the Year and Song of the Year in 1979. The Stranger made Joel an album star, not only a singles artist. The marriage did not last, ending in divorce in 1982, but the song became a wedding standard anyway. A producer's patience, a loyal band and a ballad that almost got cut turned a struggling singer into a star.

stories.title: Elton and John at the Garden
stories.dek: Thanksgiving 1974, a lost bet and a Beatle on stage
stories.body:
On Thanksgiving night, November 28, 1974, Madison Square Garden was full for Elton John's concert. Few in the crowd knew what was about to happen. In 1974 John Lennon was deep in the long separation from Yoko Ono that he later called his lost weekend. He was making an album in New York, Walls and Bridges, and Elton had joined in, playing piano and singing harmony on a song called "Whatever Gets You thru the Night".

The two made a friendly wager. Lennon did not think the single would be a big hit. Elton said that if it reached No. 1, Lennon would have to join him on stage at the Garden. When the single topped the American chart in mid-November, Lennon kept his word, though he was reportedly so nervous that he felt sick beforehand.

Elton introduced his guest to the crowd, and the roar was enormous. Lennon stepped up and played guitar on "Whatever Gets You thru the Night". He and Elton then did their version of "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", a Beatles song that Elton had just released as a single with Lennon on guitar and backing vocals under the pseudonym Dr. Winston O'Boogie.

Then came the final song. Lennon dedicated it to an old estranged fiancé of his named Paul. He launched into "I Saw Her Standing There", with the same rocking energy that the Beatles had brought to their first album.

Backstage, Yoko Ono was waiting. She had come to the show, and Lennon is said to have been moved when she sent a gardenia to his dressing room. The two reconciled in the months that followed, and Lennon returned to their home in New York early in 1975.

The night is widely described as Lennon's last full concert appearance. A short time later he stopped touring, becoming a full-time father when his son Sean was born in October 1975. The recording of the Garden show circulated for years, a rare chance to hear a Beatle on a big stage with a friend.

stories.title: Motown 25
stories.dek: The night Michael Jackson slid backward into history
stories.body:
In March 1983 a television special called Motown 25: Yesterday, Today, Forever was taped at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium. Berry Gordy, who had founded Motown in Detroit in 1959, wanted to bring back as many of his stars as he could. Diana Ross and the Supremes reunited for part of the night. The Temptations and Four Tops traded songs, and Marvin Gaye sang "What's Going On". Smokey Robinson and Stevie Wonder were there. The comedian Richard Pryor was the host.

Michael Jackson was a harder get. He had left Motown for Epic Records, and his new album, Thriller, was already on the radio. He agreed to join his brothers for a medley of Jackson 5 hits, including Jermaine, who had stayed with the label when the others left, and he said he would come only if he could also sing a new song by himself. Gordy agreed.

After the group medley, Jackson stood alone on the stage in a black sequined jacket, short black trousers, white socks and a single glittering glove. He told the crowd that those old songs were great, but that he liked the new ones better. Then he launched into "Billie Jean".

For a few seconds he did something that looked like gliding backward while appearing to walk forward. It was the moonwalk, a step that street dancers had used for years, and Jackson, who had picked it up from dancers such as Jeffrey Daniel of the group Shalamar, made it his own. The audience gasped and then roared. He has said that the great dancer Fred Astaire phoned him the next day to tell him he was a hell of a mover.

The show aired on NBC in May 1983 and drew a huge audience. Jackson's performance was the moment that people talked about at school and at work the next morning. It made "Billie Jean" more than a hit record, since it was now something people had to see. The video that had already begun to play on MTV took on new life.

Years later, Motown 25 is remembered for the reunions and the music, but above all for one man in a fedora who made a single sliding step into a piece of pop history.

covers.title: The Twist
covers.note: Hank Ballard wrote it and released it as a B side in 1959. Checker's version went to number one in 1960 and again in 1962.

covers.title: (They Long to Be) Close to You
covers.note: Burt Bacharach and Hal David wrote it, and the actor Richard Chamberlain recorded it in 1963. The Carpenters' 1970 version went to number one in the US.

covers.title: Blue Velvet
covers.note: Tony Bennett had a hit with it in 1951. Vinton's 1963 version went to number one in the US.

covers.title: Wild Thing
covers.note: Chip Taylor wrote it, and the Wild Ones, a New York group, released it in 1965. The Troggs' version reached number one in the US in 1966.

covers.title: Angel of the Morning
covers.note: Chip Taylor wrote it, and Evie Sands recorded it in 1967, but her label's troubles reportedly hurt its release. Merrilee Rush had the hit in 1968, and Juice Newton revived it in 1981.

covers.title: Spanish Harlem
covers.note: Jerry Leiber and Phil Spector wrote it, and Ben E. King recorded it in 1960. Franklin's 1971 version reached the US top three.

covers.title: Crying
covers.note: Orbison and Joe Melson wrote it, and Orbison's 1961 single reached number two in the US. McLean's version, from his album Chain Lightning, went to number one in the UK in 1980.

covers.title: I'm into Something Good
covers.note: Gerry Goffin and Carole King wrote it, and Earl-Jean, a member of the Cookies, released it in 1964. Herman's Hermits, fronted by Peter Noone, had a UK number one with it later that year.
